newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway unlikely to raise rates before Sept - poll.
newsitem.headline: Norway unlikely to raise rates before Sept - poll.

text.p: Norway's central bank, Norges Bank, is unlikely to increase official interest rates before parliamentary elections in September, economists said on Friday.
In a Reuter poll of eight Norwegian and international economists, two-thirds said they saw little to no chance of a rise in official rates.
Speculation about higher official rates has mounted over the past week because of a steep climb of between 40 and 50 basis points in money market rates.
Short rates began ascending last Thursday after the central bank set an interest rate of 3.6 percent for the period July 1 to July 14 for its fixed-term deposit rate.
Norges Bank regularly announces fixed-term deposits or fixed-term loans, which usually are carried out through ordinary auction, in order to control money market liquidity.

The bank said the fixing of a deposit rate was an attempt to carefully align money market rates up to the level of comparable ECU rates following a "normalisation" of conditions in the foreign exchange market for the crown.
Since then the bank has set a series of fixed-term rates and the three-month swap rate has surged to around 3.90 percent.

Economists say the bank has been testing the market's reaction to higher rates, while renewing its authority to control the crown. They said the bank's play had effectively hiked interest rates but without going "public" by raising official rates.

"The central bank apparently has its mind set to get interest rates higher. Short-term rates are up by around 40 basis points since last Thursday, I could see another 20 to 25 (basis) points," Knut Anton Mork, chief economist at Handelsbanken in Oslo, told Reuters.
"The interesting point is whether it will go for an official rise. It seems a little silly to keep raising market market rates without giving any signal out to the rest of the economy."

Norway's official deposit rate is 3.25 percent and the overnight lending rate is 5.25 percent. Norges Bank was forced to cut official rates at the end of 1996 and early this year to try and halt a surge in the crown. Norway's monetary is geared towards stabilising the crown versus European currencies .

Since then the crown has fallen more than seven percent against the inverse European Currency Unit (ECU) index. Analysts say the bank, by fine tuning money market rates, has taken a step-by-step approach to stabilise the currency.
The crown, however, has strengthened since the bank set the first fixed-term rate from 103.5 against the ECU index and 4.2050 versus the mark to 102.95 and 4.1650 respectively.
"An official rate hike would give a very strong signal to the market and could result in increasing interest for the crown," said Audun Gleinsvik, chief economist at Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse.
"If the crown were to appreciate again, the central bank could be forced to cut rates again and that would mean a large loss of prestige."

Analysts say, however, that the issue of a rate rise is not only based on economics. Norway will hold elections in September and recent opinion polls show that the ruling Labour Party has been losing ground to centrist parties.
Jon Rinde, senior economist at Union Bank of Norway, said he thought political decisions would rule over economic.

"The central bank appears to want to raise rates, but we believe that the central bank has to consult the government. It is not in such a free position and the government doesn't want to raise rates now," Rinde said.
"I think it is 60/40 against them raising rates, but it's getting closer."
